title: Supersonic passenger flight stalled for fifty years — the bottleneck was the engine, not aerodynamics
dek: Concorde was banned not because the technology failed, but because the sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban disappears. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and now it's being used first to generate power for data centers.
why: The founder's own account of the full path from being turned down by Bezos to building his own engine and pivoting to data-center power generation, with specific numbers and regulatory detail, high information density.
who: Founders and investors focused on hard tech, aviation and data-center energy, especially those who want to see how a hardware company uses another market to feed its main business.
skip: The opening 0:00-4:10 is launch-event-style setup and a promo video; skip to 5:12 for the main topic.

points.h: Bend the sonic boom and the ban disappears
points.body: Boom's solution to the sonic boom is not to make the aircraft quiet, but to use the atmosphere's own refractive capacity to redirect the boom back into the sky. Blake calls this boomless cruise; engineers call it Mach cutoff: the boom is still generated by the aircraft, at normal strength, but it bends sharply in the air and never reaches the ground. This works below Mach 1.3, which is 50% faster than today. So you can't go full speed over land, but a 9 a.m. departure from New York and a 9:30 a.m. arrival in San Francisco still holds. Over the ocean no one is listening, so full speed is fine. Taken to its logical extreme: if there's no boom at all, there's nothing to argue about.

points.h: From executive order to congressional law, unanimous
points.body: The U.S. ban on supersonic flight over land, in place since 1973, ended on June 6 last year. But Blake knew an executive order could in theory be overturned by the next person, so he turned to pushing congressional legislation. The Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House unanimously and recently cleared a Senate committee unanimously as well. He put the significance plainly: supersonic isn't a partisan issue, which is how you get those vote counts. For a hardware company that needs to span multiple administrations and whose cycles are measured in decades, upgrading regulation from executive order to law turns policy risk from a variable into a constant.

points.h: Getting stood up by a big company saved the company
points.body: Blake says one of the dumbest things he ever did was outsource engine development to an established large company; the plan failed, there was a public split with Rolls-Royce, and everyone said Boom was finished. So they decided to do what everyone said was impossible: build the engine from scratch themselves, and not just design it — even the hardest parts, like turbine blades, they make themselves. His judgment: engineering and manufacturing must be done together; if you want to reindustrialize America, you have to invent the next generation of manufacturing technology here, not bring back what was offshored to China. That forced choice later became the source of the company's valuation — because an engine designed for Mach 1.7 high-temperature full-power long-duration operation, with the front fan removed and a generator attached at the back, is a power generation device.

points.h: The supersonic engine's first customer is a data center
points.body: Boom's engine's first application isn't in the sky, it's on the ground. Remove the fan, swap in a generator at the back, put it in a few trailers, and you can do 42 megawatts of behind-the-meter generation, and because the engine core is designed to run at high temperature, it doesn't need water. Blake specifically points out that water is a common objection, so just make it disappear. The factory has already started producing the first parts, with a target of multiple gigawatts a year and adding more than 10 gigawatts to the grid over the next five years. The financial significance of this path: before the supersonic airliner gets its airworthiness certificate, the company already has a product it can sell, and it's selling to the buyer with the least shortage of money right now.

points.h: Run on the ground first, then fly
points.body: Boom using the engine first for ground power generation has an engineering side effect: it will be the most-tested new jet engine in history, because it will have run for a huge number of hours on the ground before ever being installed and flown. Blake admits many hard problems remain and success isn't guaranteed. The promise to passengers: twice as fast over water, 50% faster over land with no sonic boom. The sequencing itself is worth noting — normally aviation engine validation relies on accumulating flight hours; Boom has moved validation to the ground and data-center scenarios, effectively using another market to pay the test costs for the aviation business.

The numbers Blake gives: Mach 1.7 transatlantic round trip in 3 hours, breakeven fare around $3,500, actual ticket price probably higher, and every extra dollar is United's profit. His assessment of Concorde: zero out of three on safe, comfortable and cheap; Boom aims to get all three. On timeline, the target is 4 years, but he states clearly that ‘fast is more important than predictable’, can't give a definite date, and only promises to deliver at the earliest time physically possible, which outsiders read as around 2030. There's a trade-off worth noting here: a hardware company publicly admitting it's unpredictable, trading certainty for speed.

points.h: Data-center demand is so large it will be auctioned
points.body: Asked whether the data-center business is a money printer, Blake's answer is ‘it's the most incredible money-printing business I've ever seen’, and says his inbox has tens of gigawatts of demand. The first engine will fire up next month, and then they plan to auction off all the capacity. Asked whether he's talked to Elon, or whether it's for Colossus, Blake only says ‘you should ask Elon’. The value of this segment is that it gives a counterintuitive supply-demand signal: for a power product not yet in mass production, demand already far exceeds capacity, and the pricing method has shifted from a quote to an auction.

points.h: Break the sound barrier Monday, model in the Oval Office Thursday
points.body: Blake recaps the speed of this regulatory push: Monday, break the sound barrier, tweet, Elon retweets, that night fly to Washington to start the legalization lobbying, and by landing he already had a White House invitation; Tuesday, into the West Wing; Thursday, the aircraft model went into the Oval Office, and it's still there. From launch to signature, the executive order took 115 days, which he thinks is slow, but admits would be slower under a different administration. His assessment of this administration: ‘I like that it moves fast’. This is the most concrete policy-operations sample in the whole episode: how a technical milestone gets directly converted into political attention.
